introduction: This Third Sunday of Advent is called Gaudete Sunday, from the Latin word for rejoice, and rose vestments may be worn. Isaiah announces good news to the poor, Mary sings that her spirit rejoices in God her Saviour, and Paul tells us to rejoice always. In the Gospel, John the Baptist says that among us stands one we do not recognise. As we celebrate, let us rejoice, for the Lord is near.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Rejoicing that the Lord is near, let us bring our prayers to the Father with thankful hearts.
intentions: For the Church: that she may be a joyful witness to Christ, bringing good news to the poor and healing to the broken-hearted. Let us pray to the Lord.
For prisoners, captives and all who are not free: that they may find release and hope in God. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who find this season hard, especially the grieving, the lonely and the sick: that the Lord may give them a deep and quiet joy. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who have lost faith: that they may recognise Christ, who stands among us even when we do not see him. Let us pray to the Lord.
For our community: that we may rejoice always, pray without ceasing and give thanks in all things. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: God of joy, your Son is close at hand. Fill our hearts with the gladness of his coming, and answer the prayers we offer in faith. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Joy that does not depend on circumstances
reflection.body:
Halfway through Advent, the Church lightens the colour of her vestments and speaks of joy. The readings are full of it. Isaiah's servant announces good news to the humble, healing for the broken-hearted and freedom for captives. Mary takes the place of the psalm: "My soul magnifies the Lord. My spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior."

Paul's instruction to the Thessalonians is three short lines: "Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you." It sounds impossible. How can anyone rejoice always, in illness, debt or grief?

The answer is that Christian joy is not the same as happiness. Happiness depends on what happens to us; joy depends on who is with us. Paul wrote these words to a young church already facing persecution. Mary sang her song while carrying a child in difficult and uncertain circumstances. Their joy came from the faithfulness of God, which remains when everything else is shaken.

In the Gospel, priests and Levites come to question John the Baptist. Who are you? Are you the Messiah, Elijah, the prophet? John refuses every title. "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness," he says. Then he adds something remarkable: "among you stands one whom you don't know." Christ is already present, unrecognised in the crowd.

That is still true. Christ stands among us in the Eucharist, in his word, in the poor, and in the quiet events of our days. Part of Advent is learning to recognise him. When we do, joy follows, even in hard times.

Paul's three lines can become a simple rule for the rest of Advent: begin each day with thanksgiving, turn small moments into brief prayers, and look for one reason to rejoice before going to sleep. The Lord is near.
